utterances.text: During the time you were at Batkovic, did the ICRC visit the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in command when this first visit occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Veljo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When this first visit occurred, was it the first visit that the inmates of the camp were registered by the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to this visit, to your knowledge, were any of the camp inmates taken away from the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were these people who were taken away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were mostly people over 60 years of age and children below the age of 16, and those who had been battered badly before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a special group of men in the camp who received worse treatment than others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men were in this group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the men who were taken away that day, did you know any of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnic group of those that you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the inmates told what to say when the ICRC arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they gave us instructions what we were to say when they came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had to say that we were fine in the camp; that the food was great; that nobody was beating us; that they were giving us cigarettes; that we could move around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all those things true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would happen if you did not say those things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one who did not obey was battered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 21st July 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was it that you were allowed to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left the camp through the mediation of the ICRC and the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the attack on Rogatica, were you a member of an anti-Serb military or paramilitary organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to that attack were you a member of any organised anti-Serb resistance group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the attack on Rogatica, were you a member of any of these types of organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes, please. (11.34 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You had completed direct, Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have some cross-examination of this witness. Cross-examined by MR. KAY

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first matter I would like to detail with is uniforms. You have told us that originally you were in the regular military police, is that right, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in the regular military police during 1987. How long did you serve in the JNA regular military police for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The regular JNA military police, I served from 17th September 1986 to 17th August 1987, eleven months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The uniform that you describe as having worn for that year, did that remain the uniform of the regular JNA military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After my service in the JNA ended, that uniform remained the regular uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then joined the Reserve military police, but it did not require a great deal of your time because it was only concerned with duties amounting to one or two days each year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you issued with a separate uniform then for the Reserve military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Special uniform for the Reserve military police I received in the beginning of 1988.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe that uniform to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That uniform was identical with the uniform of the traffic military police, except that it was grey rather than grey, olive green.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were then called up to join the regular police in September 1991. By "regular police" do you mean the ordinary police of the town rather than the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The regular police uniform that you were issued with, what did that consist of, what was its colour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the same uniform I was issued in the beginning of 1988, that is, the same military uniform except that it was grey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Except that it was grey; would it not be the case that it was the same in colour because the Reserve military police uniform was grey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Were there also Reserve police who were issued with a uniform, not being part of the regular police but Reserve Police Forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of us who were issued these uniforms were part of the regular police as the Reserve force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Reserve police also wore a grey uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told us that you were issued with a weapon, an automatic rifle; was the Reserve police also issued with weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were all issued automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is, the Reserve police as well as the regular police were issued with weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as of September 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described being issued with 150 bullets as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have to sign for these weapons from the department or the section of the police that issued them to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I signed both for the weapons and the equipment I was issued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there would be a record of the issue of this weapon to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The record was issued before the war; whether there are any now, I would not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Can you tell us again the date when you resigned from the regular police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on 30th March 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your resignation was to whom? Who did you go to see to tell them that you did not want to continue in the regular police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time there was the deputy police commander. He was in the building of the police station, and I told him that I did not want to be part of the police any longer and I gave my uniform and weapons back to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any others in the regular police who also resigned at the same time as you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A friend of mine resigned. He was also on the Reserve police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before your resignation, had others also resigned from the regular police over the months beforehand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Except for the people of Serb ethnic origin who left the police station and joined the Serb police, the police of the Serb Republic, nobody else resigned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, can you give as an idea then of the numbers that remained in the regular police that you had previously been a part of? How many were acting as policemen for the regular police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Including the Reserve and active duty policemen, there were some 50 men in the regular Police Force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us about the division of the police and the formation of the Serbian police unit. How many people worked for that unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the exact number of those who worked for the police of the Serb Republic because I was never there, that is, I was never part of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you again a little bit more about the uniform that would have been worn at that time by the regular police. First of all, the head wear, caps or berets, what was the head wear that was worn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The regular police who received -- who were paid for the duty, they wore caps with a shield. The Reserve police had military caps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the uniform remain the same at this time, in March 1992, at the time of your resignation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As regards regular Police Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the uniform remained the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Reserve police, that uniform remained the same as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had your own pistol that you kept in your house that you told us of this morning; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a licensed weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had had that for how long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That pistol belonged to my father and when he died in 1985, in April, I inherited the pistol and from that time until the beginning of the war I had it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us about the distribution of weapons amongst the population in your town. You said that the Muslim population were carrying no weapons ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- yet you told us subsequently that there were some 50 Muslim people who did have weapons and who were giving resistance at the time that the town was attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Individuals who did have weapons and resisted at the time were using weapons, their own weapons they had as hunting weapons or small firearms, so that is mostly pistols.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know this? How do you know that they only had hunting weapons or their own pistols?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I was near that part where these people were and I could see the kind of weapons they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it comes to this: you did, in fact, see Muslims carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw Muslims carrying weapons as of 22nd May 1992 -- not before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before that time, had there been any areas of your town that had been cordoned off by some of the Muslim population with their own road blocks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had there been any mobilization of the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On 22nd May then when you say you saw these people with weapons, whereabouts were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 22nd May, I was in my flat and after that I once went to this square, to the town square, where most of the Muslim people were and that is where I saw those people with weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many days after 22nd May was it that you went to the square?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two or three days after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the two or three days before you went to the square, had you left your flat at all? I believe you said you were in the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent in the cellar most of the time and I did not leave it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that time had you heard gun shots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you also heard louder explosions than gun shots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard shelling, the echoes of shells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear detonations as if bombs were exploding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Slightly smaller detonations as if hand grenades were exploding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This activity was taking place where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the territory of the town of Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your apartment was in the town itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The explosions that were taking place, were they explosions that you could hear from all parts of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was in the cellar of my building, and when I heard those explosions it seemed to me that those explosions were taking place in front of my building, but during intermissions, during the brief breaks, between the shellings, when I would go up to my flat I could see that a large part or the central part of the town had been destroyed which meant that explosions were coming from that direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard the sound of gun shots. Did you hear the sounds of machine guns or did you hear the sounds of rifles or small arms fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The shots I heard were mostly from automatic weapons and they came in bursts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not know what was taking place where that fighting was happening? You did not know what was happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I knew then that the town was being shelled, that the town was being destroyed; nothing else. I could gather that from the place where I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did not know who was fighting whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew who was shelling the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were inside your basement, your cellar of your apartment, so, presumably, you could not see what was happening with shelling, where it was coming from, who was doing it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the night the shelling would stop, and then with my family I would go up to my flat for reasons of hygiene and food, of course, and while I would be in the flat shelling would start again. Out of the window I could clearly see light bullets and the shells and what direction they were coming from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was night-time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to fighting that was taking place then, you were not actually there at the time to see what was happening; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could not see if Muslims were, in fact, fighting the others because you were not there, you were not there watching fighting taking place? You were in your flat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have said, some 50 individuals in the central square were armed mostly with hunting rifles and pistols, and the town was shelled from nearby clearings or hills with artillery and anti-aircraft weaponry; and I really see no purpose how it can people with rifles defend themselves against artillery or anti-aircraft weapons firing from that distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thought you told us that you saw in this square two or three days later about 50 Muslims with weapons at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did see those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the time before then, did you see those same people fighting in the square shooting their weapons in that period of the two or three days before you saw them in the square?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see those people shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what you did see two or three days later were a number of people, about 50 in number, with weapons in the square?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as to what other people were doing with weapons elsewhere previously, you yourself did not see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Re-examined by MISS HOLLIS

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, let us talk a moment about the way the police were organised in the former Yugoslavia. We understand that the JNA was organised into an active duty component and a Reserve component. Is it your testimony that the police were also organised into some type of active duty component, that is, full-time regular policemen and a Reserve component?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a member of this Reserve component; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was the members of the Reserve police component who wore the grey uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The members of this active duty component, if you will, of the police, what colour was their uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Trousers were grey, shirts light blue, and jackets blue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, the shirts were blue, the jackets were blue, that was the active duty police; and the Reserve police wore all grey in their uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In September 1991 when you began to work each day as a policeman, were you still a Reserve policeman or had you become a part of the active duty component?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a Reserve policeman but I worked full-time like active duty forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were being asked about hearing detonations and explosions and volleys of firing while you were in the cellar, you indicated that at one point you came up and you were able to observe that most of the destruction was in the central part of the city; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, as of 22nd May, what group or groups were still living in the central part of the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Inhabitants who lived in the centre of the town were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had there at one time prior to 22nd May also been Serbs who had lived in the central part of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that part of the town before 22nd May, I might say April and before that, there was a mixed population made of Serbs and Muslims. In early May, in the first half of May, the Serb population left that part of the town and all those parts of the town where the Muslims made up the majority, they all moved to those parts of the town where there were Serbs living or went out of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also testified that at some point you were able to come up from the cellar at night-time and you observed firing at night. I believe you indicated that you saw tracer rounds coming into the town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what area were these tracer rounds coming?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those tracer rounds came from a village inhabited mostly by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I have one question to ask about the digging of trenches. You told us that you dug trenches at the front. Were you a volunteer? Did you volunteer to dig those trenches or were you compelled to dig them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, during my stay in the Batkovic camp, that is, as of the day when I was captured to the day of my release, I had no right to do anything of my own will. I was compelled to do all that I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The others with you who also were digging trenches, were they in the same position as you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the inmates were in the same, in the identical, position as I was; they had no right to decide on anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you mentioned that when the ICRC people visited the detention centre, you were told to tell them things that did not really happen in your experience, and you said that those who refused to tell them what they were told to say were beaten. Were there occasions when some of your colleagues refused to tell them as they were instructed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you testified that 66 per cent of the population of Rogatica were Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 66 per cent in the municipality of Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And in the city the ratio was 62 to 37.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a mayor of Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had a mayor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the mayor in 1990/1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you need his name?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, just really what political party.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He belonged to the SDA and he was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were the elections that led to his becoming the mayor, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took place in 1991. I would not know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the SDA win most of the positions for the town government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SDA won 20 seats in the town government of the total of 50. The Muslims, that is, people of Muslim origin who were Council men accounted for -- no, 30 of -- of 50 Council men, 30 were Muslims; there were 20 Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Muslims were in political control, I gather, then of Rogatica in 1991, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Muslims won the elections in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that at the end of 1991, or the beginning of 1992, you began to see an increase in the JNA. Did you actually see a number of troops of the JNA in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I noticed a group of JNA or, rather, columns of the Yugoslav People's Army passing through the town and sometimes staying for a day or two on the outskirts of the town. It did not happen before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the JNA leave any of their equipment with them after they would leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On passing through, they would fire at the town so that is part of the equipment, but I did not see that they had left anything behind -- at least, I did not see it myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to determine what type of uniforms they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Grey olive military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the SMB uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: SMB uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When this Serb autonomous area was established in the spring of 1992, do you know how it came to be established? Was there an election or can you tell me how this autonomous area was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, that autonomous region was established with the help of the Serb Democratic Party that was present in the area without any elections. They simply organised themselves and proclaimed that region and everything that went with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Muslims and Serbs live primarily in different parts of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two or three parts of the town were purely either Muslim or Serb, but in most parts of the town they lived together, so it was mixed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the area where the autonomous region was declared, the Serb autonomous region, was that an area occupied exclusively by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The whole area of the municipality of Rogatica was included in there without asking anybody or asking anyone's permission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what were the geographical boundaries of the semi-autonomous area that was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The geographical boundaries were the territories of the opstinas of Pale, Sokolac, Han Pijesak and Rogatica. I am not sure, I think also the area of the municipality of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I am trying to determine is where this semi-autonomous Serb region was established in the spring -- was it the spring of 1992 -- where in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was established mostly in parts of the opstina of Rogatica where mostly lived Serb inhabitants, because there was no way that anyone would be against it in those parts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any Muslims living in that area at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they lived but in small numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they remain in that area after it was declared to be a semi-autonomous area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them remained; some of them had to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the head of the police department in the spring of 1992 when it was divided? Was he a Croat, a Muslim, a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The head of the Police Force the day before the division was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you still with the police at that point? You resigned in, was it, March 1992 or May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same day when the police department was divided, that is, on 30th March 1992, I left the police department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave an order to divide the police department, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The order for the division of the police department was issued by the Serb municipality of Rogatica, and the Serb Crisis Committee which had been established in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Muslim Chief of Police followed that order, is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, nobody asked him anything, because the policemen who were Serbs by nationality, they were told to divide and to leave the regular police. So they divided these two police stations and established a new one out of their own will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that they then wore camouflage uniforms with an emblem of the Serb Republic on it, the new unit of the police, the Serb unit that separated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, most of them wore such uniforms although, to begin with, they looked in a pretty disorganised way, so some people wore these SMB uniforms at first or they were even wearing civilian clothes, but on their arms they had an emblem showing that they belonged to the Serb police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you seen this emblem of the Serb Republic before this division of the police department, or before you testified that you were at a checkpoint and you saw a civilian vehicle with licence plates from Macedonia, I believe, and you said that you saw some persons in a uniform in that car with a Serb Republic emblem, had you seen that emblem before that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Such an emblem, I could see from time to time while I was working at a restaurant because uniformed people would come there and I could see them wear such an emblem, but that was at the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What uniforms did the soldiers who were in the Serb unit headed by Kusic, is it, what uniform did they wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly they wore SMB camouflage uniforms and wearing red -- I am sorry, black berets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the Crisis Committee headquarters is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Crisis Headquarters Committee, this is a group of people that were to organise the people that are in danger in any kind of way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the head of it? I thought you had testified that Mr. Kusic established the Crisis Headquarters, and at that time he was the head of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Rajko Kusic founded the brigade. He was a member of the SDS party. He was one of the leaders. He founded the Serb opstina and he was one of the most prominent people of the Crisis Headquarters. I do not know whether he was the head of it, but he was one of the most prominent people there because -- I do not, I cannot tell you more about it. I do not know whether he was really the head of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the Crisis Committee Headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, the purpose was that all the Serb population in the Rogatica opstina would get organised in the best possible way, meaning that all the population aged between 16 and 65 that were able to fight, they should be included and organised in such kinds of activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that established, that Crisis Committee Headquarters, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was established in the spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis, additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Further re-examined by MISS HOLLIS

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, as I understand it from your testimony, the Serb autonomous region was composed of several opstinas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the Serb autonomous region composed of the entire part of each opstina, or only those portions of the opstina in which Serbs lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the Serb autonomous region of Romanija was established, the creation were called people from the Serb Democratic Party, that is, the people who were Serb, and they established that region which included all the opstinas I mentioned, and regardless of the territory, that means that the Serb autonomous region was comprised of the entire areas of all the opstinas that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So both the Serb and the non-Serb areas of those opstinas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it included all the areas. They did not ask anyone from those areas whether they wanted to join or not into that region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that same regard, I believe you testified that after some seven days of shelling a group came into the city of Rogatica, into the town, and demanded that the Muslims there take a loyalty oath; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a loyalty oath to whom? To whom were they to be loyal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had to be loyal towards the Serb opstina of Rogatica and the power, the authorities of that opstina, which meant that the Muslims should leave all the authority in the opstina of Rogatica to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nothing arising.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. You may be excused. Thank you very much for coming. Any objection to being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Pasic you may leave. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Miss Sutherland could return Prosecution Exhibit 73?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution's next witness is Hanne Sophie Greve. However, I understand the Defence wishes to raise an objection with the court prior to her taking the stand.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour I mentioned this sometime ago when this witness was on the list concerning her testimony, that there be objection in part to what she has to say. In those circumstances, it is a matter of law that we should properly deal with before she is sworn and so that the court has an idea to the nature of the objection. Your Honour, I have had a brief bundle for the court relating to the matters that I raise and I am looking for someone to -- (documents handed). Before we go into that, may I perhaps outline the nature of the evidence that this witness is proposed to give. We have been provided with a proffer of testimony on behalf of this witness which is a summary of what it is proposed that she will deal with over the day or so that she has been listed on the Prosecution schedule. In addition to that, her purpose of being called is in a capacity of an expert witness and we have been supplied with a copy of her curriculum vitae. We are aware of the role that she has played in relation to the background of this case, because she prepared a report for the United Nations specifically on the Prijedor area as a matter of research. I do not know how familiar the court is with that, but we certainly have it with us. This morning the Prosecution supplied me with extracts from that report which are specific matters that she will be referring to in giving evidence amounting to some 60 pages or so Now we are in the position here of objection being taken on the basis of the kind of evidence that this witness will be giving as an expert, but to do that it is very difficult to address the court in the abstract, being the judges as of law as well as the judges of fact. This is a witness who will be seeking to present before the court various materials prepared by her in the preparation of her report for the United Nations in support of her testimony. I am going to have to feel my way as to how far the Tribunal can look at her proposed testimony which we are seeking to exclude from the evidence before the court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why are you seeking to exclude her testimony and what portions of her testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: She is being called as an expert witness who is giving evidence relating to reports and research undertaken by her; interviews with perhaps witnesses who are to be called by the Prosecution in this case or other witnesses who have been involved with events before the court, as well as detailed extracts from books that have been published, books that are on popular sale, one by a gentleman called Mr. Vulliamy and another Prosecution witness, newspaper reports ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me, if I may, interrupt you one moment. Perhaps the best way to approach this is to hear from the Prosecutor first to determine who this witness is, what they expect her testimony to be and then let me hear your objection. I am trying to put it in a proper framework and I have not yet gotten to why you are objecting. I think it is because of what she will testify to, but I know nothing about her other than her name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is the problem that I indicated to the court in dealing with the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sure, you mentioned the name, but you did not tell us anything about the witness or what would be the basis of the objection. So if we can just hear generally what the testimony would be then and then you tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. The witness is Hanne Sophie Greve who is a judge of the Court of Appeals of Norway, also a trial judge, with extensive experience in humanitarian law investigations with international conflicts, and was appointed to the Commission of Experts which was established pursuant to UN Resolution under the Security Council's powers under Chapter VII, and who in the course of her work with the Commission focused on the Prijedor region and, indeed, did initiate an independent stud of that region in conjunction with her examination and evaluation of all other available materials. The Commission of Experts' Resolution called upon international humanitarian organisations to collate and present to the Commission all available materials on the conflict, of course including Prijedor. In addition to reviewing and evaluating that, she undertook a very specific investigation into the Prijedor region, part of which consisted of interviews with witnesses, indeed approximately 400 witnesses, who were interviewed by police officers and legal officials and government officials in six different countries around the world. If I can put her proposed testimony in proper context, I take the Court back to Dr. Gow's testimony and remind the court that Dr. Gow was asked some specific questions about Prijedor both by the Defence and by the Court. He properly demurred, noting that his expertise concerned the region as a whole and the conflict as a whole and, therefore, not specific areas of the conflict. The Court expressed, I think, an understandable and reasonable expectation that someone would follow who was an expert about that region. That is precisely who Judge Greve is and what we propose she testifies about.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Tell me again, what is her expertise? I understand she is a judge. I understand she has experience in human rights. I gather that -- was she working with the Commission of Experts?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: She was one of the Commissioners.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And she interviewed a number of individuals. Of course, in your system you would offer the witness as an expert in?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The conflict in Prijedor, its background and nature and the extent of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: She will base her testimony on interviews that she conducted or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Interviews that were conducted at her behest by professionals, lawyers, police officers, government officials in six different countries, in almost 400 of those, interviews that were conducted by government officials in other places, so, perhaps another 100 of those; on every document and the materials which were presented pursuant to the Resolution which established the Commission; on contact with embassies and government officials, from both Serbian, Bosnian and Croatian sources -- I could go on. Basically every possible contact she could make that would shed light on the conflict she made.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Now, your objection, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a witness being called to relay the reports that others have provided for her and for her to give conclusions to this court in relation to those reports and documents that she has been supplied with which are, in effect, usurping the role of this Court, which is to make findings of fact in relation to the events that took place in the Prijedor region. So, what we have here is not a witness with a technical, scientific or any other expertise who would supply knowledge to assist the Court in relation to matters that the Court may not otherwise understand and need guidance upon, but she is being presented as a witness who, as a result of her research interviews being conducted by others that have been relayed to her (and we do not know what process of language it has gone through to get to her) including a number of Prosecution witnesses, that are not matters that this Court will need expert guidance upon, because the assessment of the witnesses that decisions concerning what was happening in Prijedor are matters of judgment that the Tribunal is there to supply and we say the Tribunal is well able to supply. It does not need a witness to come along as an expert to say: "I have had provided to me the interviews of some 400 witnesses. I can tell you that, as a result of reading newspapers, as a result of speaking to journalists and reading books on the matter, I can advise the Court that there was a conflict in Prijedor, that this act was committed against one section of the population, by another section of the population and these events took place in this form." The nature of our objection is rather fundamental. It encompasses whether expert opinion is needed on this matter as well as any hearsay reports from witnesses who were actually experiencing those events at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can you point the Trial Chamber to any particular rule of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence which will govern the trial and this Chamber, can you point us to any rule that you consider supports your position that this evidence should be excluded?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall we turn to Rule 89 which is really the governing rule in relation to rules of evidence

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Rule 89?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Rule 89(A) makes a point we all know very well, that the Tribunal is not bound by national rules of evidence. Subparagraph (b): "In cases not otherwise provided for in this section, a Chamber shall apply Rules of Evidence which will best favour a fair determination of the matter before it and are consonant with the spirit of the Statute and the general principles of law; (c) A Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value; (d) a Chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial." What the Tribunal has been told this morning is that the evidence that this witness is proposed to give is the result of her research, having had numerous discussions with other people, and I can tell the Court, having seen the list of documents presented to me this morning, including extracts from publications by journalists and including extracts from books, newspaper reports. So what we are having here is a witness being called to say: "I have spoken and I have read about these matters and I can tell you what I have been told."

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is your objection that their testimony will in part be based on hearsay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We come into the hearsay realm straightaway, and one does not know how many hands of hearsay; it may well be second, third fourth-hand of hearsay. Furthermore, looking at Rule 89 which has regard to evidence which will best favour a fair determination of the matter before it and are consonant with the spirit of the Statute and the general principles of law, I ask the Court to go straight to principle so that we can consider, perhaps, why in many jurisdictions such an approach would be objectionable on the basis of it, first of all, providing hearsay evidence as well as providing conclusions upon a matter where the court does not need any expertise. The purpose of this case is for the Prosecution to call evidence from witnesses as to what was happening in the Prijedor region and what took place, what their experiences were and what events were that were leading up to those experiences. The Court has seen that the list of witnesses. There are a substantial number who will be giving eyewitness testimony as to what happened and relating their direct experiences. I have provided the court this morning with a small bundle. In fact, the first two pages are the pages where I set out in very brief form the principle that is concerned. It is headed "Opinion Evidence". It was the first document in the bundle supplied to the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have it. You have referred us to Rule 89, of course, which is the general provisions governing our Rules of Evidence. As you know, we do not have a rule that governs the testimony of expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: There is a reference to an expert witness being allowed to testify. Of course, in Rule 90, which is entitled "Testimony of Witnesses", and that is 90(D), it says: "A witness other than an expert" etc., "shall not be present when the testimony of another witness is given." So we do not have a rule that -- and we of course are close to a recess, so I imagine the best thing to do is to take this material you have given us which are excerpts from various publications regarding expert evidence, we can take that and look at it -- we do not have a rule that deals with expert testimony and does not set out the parameters of expert testimony. In my system, of course -- and this is very interesting because out of all the lawyers probably Mr. Tieger is the only one who comes from my system; of course Mr. Niemann is from Judge Stephen's system and I think Judge Vohrah has a lot of experience from your system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So, what we are asked to do I suppose is to listen to you and accept your suggestion that we apply -- I guess this is Cross and Taper on Evidence. Is that from England?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am not suggesting you apply the rules of any particular nationality.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What is the second one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is an extract from Archbold, including a case from South Australia.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Australia?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We refer to Australian cases in our evidence quite frequently. What I have done in the main paper, I have deliberately avoided referring to the National Rules of Evidence and I have sought to distil principle on the basis that principle is the best way to argue the matter because we are most concerned with that within Rule 89.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would this apply to a jury as well as a non-jury case, these principles you are advocating?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I have provided text there. I suppose lawyers feel lonely without text and authorities to support them, but I have done that as background material where argument is also set out cogently in relation to all the matters. I hope that assists the Court. It is right, it is the first time that we have had to deal with this point, but we say it is an important matter of principles. We acknowledge the fact that expert evidence is entitled to be called and we take no objection to other aspects of the Prosecution case where expert evidence will be used. What we say about this witness is that it is strays beyond the traditional band of expertise that would be required into an area of opinion and comment that is seeking to provide conclusions to the Tribunal based on research otherwise provided to it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, is there anything that you would like to provide the Chamber for us to look at over the noon recess?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not have materials to provide the court. I just received the bundle of materials immediately after the recess. I will make an effort to gather any useful material for the court's benefit during the break. However, I have a few comments, if I may. First of all, let me outline the nature of the objection here which has not been explicitly stated. The Defence is satisfied that Judge Greve testifies along the lines of the proffer given up to and including the attack on the Hambarine area in Prijedor. The objection comes to events thereafter; that includes the attack and cleansing of Kozarac, the collection of civilians, taking them to camps, conditions in camps and the periodic cleansings that followed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That I did not understand. I understood that the objection was to all of her testimony, at least in so far as if it was seeking to offer opinion evidence and, I gather, an opinion based on hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is the reference in the handout provided by the Defence in the first paragraph, "The evidence concerning matters within the experience of the witness that is relevant to the proceedings, no objection is taken", I was advised orally that that refers to portions of the proffer after paragraph 17 of the proffer. I have just related the contents of that to the court. With respect to the argument as to other matters which the Prosecution proposes the witness testify to, first of all, the Defence asserts that her testimony would usurp the rol of the court. It is not intended to usurp the role of the court, but to assist the role of the court. That is another way of referring to the rule against expert witnesses, or any other witness, testifying to the ultimate fact in issue. That is a rule which has been expressly abandoned in the United States and I think eroded to the point of extinction in many other jurisdictions. The emphasis of that rule is certainly on the jury and the concern that a jury may be so dazzled by the imprimatur of expert that they may fail to exercise their independent judgment. That is not a risk here. This witness can be cross-examined; the court can examine the witness; the court can certainly assign the weight it deems proper to the testimony of this witness. The Defence argues in its submission that this is something that need not be assisted by an expert witness, and points out in the submission, "If a cardinal of the Roman Catholic Church is testifying before a jury and states that, in his opinion, the defendant was driving negligently, it can hardly be supposed that the verdict would be other than for the plaintiff." We, unfortunately, are not dealing with a single car accident. Opstina Prijedor -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It depends whether it is in Ulster or not!

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not know that this Tribunal would be so overwhelmed even by the testimony of a cardinal. I think that we were able to separate fact from fiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Opstina Prijedor is a large area, your Honour. It is about 35 kilometres to 25 kilometres. That means from, perhaps, Scheveningen beach to the airport, from here to Rotterdam. More than 50,000 Muslims and Croats were killed or forcibly expelled from that area by a co-ordinated attack by Serbian political, military, paramilitary and Police Forces all in furtherance of the goal of creating a unified Serbian entity. If the Prosecution were to call the number of witnesses necessary to illuminate and clarify and explain the nature and extent and interrelationship of that attack, and the camps which followed which were an implementation and realisation of that goal, we will be here for a very long time indeed. The witnesses we are calling deal with specific acts -- the bulk of the witnesses we are calling deal with specific acts of the defendant. We do not propose that this witness testify about any specific acts of the defendant or specific victims. Indeed, this witness will not be going into details about the camp, but to provide the court with enough of a understanding of the camps and of the cleansings so that the court can appropriately understand the nature, extent and purpose of those events in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I ask you, do you contemplate that this witness will, among other things, give evidence which is no more than a recounting of what she has been told some of the 400 witnesses that others interviewed said?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I understand the court's question correctly, your Honour, I think the answer would be, no. She is not going to relate specific events related by one individual or two individuals. Her testimony consists of those areas where all available facts converge. That is one of the reasons why she will not be testifying about a single specific incident, because she has not investigated that single specific incident, but she has become an expert on the conflict in Prijedor. So, let us take, for example, the existence of Omarska camp: That she will testify about its existence based on a wide range of factors, including information provided by witnesses naturally, but as to a single incident which is related by a single witness, for example, she will not be a conduit for that testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I gather that what she will do is form an opinion based upon interviews of, you now say, 400 or so perhaps witnesses and say, based upon those interviews, she has an opinion as to what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I can step back a moment, your Honour, I would like to clarify that. There has been, I think, an undue focus on the interviews. I think that was an important aspect of what she did and an appropriate aspect of what she did, but it was an adjunct to everything else that was done as well. This is not a summary of what witnesses told her. It is her conclusions based on the intersection of all information available and, therefore, what can be known. I think it is fair to say that what she heard from any individual witness does not put her in a position to say: "On the basis of that single witness, or single victim, I am prepared to say that is precisely what happened". She conducted research and has become an expert on the subject in just the way, for example, Dr. Gow did, by examining all available information. The fact that interviews were conducted at her behest, should not count against her, but I think for her.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What is the conclusion that she is offering? I am sure that has been provided to the Defence in the statement. What is the conclusion she is offering?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The witness will explain the relationship between the events in Prijedor and the events that Dr. Gow talked about; the connection between Prijedor and what happened outside of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So she again is a design or policy or scheme, I guess, witness to connect the testimony that we have heard already moving it finally to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It will be in Prijedor, your Honour, and she will be testifying -- certainly her testimony will be relevant to international conflict. It will also, of course, be relevant to how widespread or systematic the attack was in Prijedor; it will be relevant to the organisations, JNA, SDS, which participated in that attack and their relations to entities outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you made no objection to Mr. Gow giving his expert opinion when he was called. In what way is the nature of the forthcoming witness' evidence to be different from Dr. Gow's?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is very different and Mr. Gow was called as a witness to give an historical perspective as a military historian and events related to the constitution. There is no objection to those aspects of this witness' testimony which would cover similar ground because it is a matter of public record, a matter of public knowledge. But we have been supplied with a proffer of testimony -- again I am feeling my way here because we are dealing with a Tribunal of fact as well as a Tribunal of law -- where the witness refers to events that took place in Kozarac which has come about as a result of her interviewing or having interviewed on her behalf witnesses. She describes, for instance, Omarska as being a virtual death camp. She describes the conditions of the prisoners. She describes physical abuse was routine. She was not there and witnesses are being called to deal with that. She describes the circumstances in which they are being held within these camps; how they were run with inspectors; the circumstances in which areas were allegedly cleansed of other populations in that area. Our submission is that these are all matters of fact for this Tribunal to listen to the witnesses and decide whether they agree or disagree. The danger in calling someone else into this courtroom to report what she has been told by others is that, I am not saying that the ultimate issue argument is something that I am putting before the court, but that conclusions are being put before the court that are really the role of the Tribunal rather than a witness to come in; where does it stop? Do produce a couple of investigators from Prijedor to come in and say, "Well, we have spoken to everyone in the region; we believe Dusko Tadic is not guilty. We have spoken to everyone, we have considered what happened and his defence is this and sound." It is where you are straying so far into issues of fact that the court does not require those expressions of opinion, but what the court requires is expertise on matters that the court, perhaps, does not have the facility to understand, which is why we refer to scientific and technological data. But here this whole section of this report, the second half, goes beyond the Gow area, which I know my learned friends objected to at the time -- I, unfortunately, was incapacitated with flu and not here -- I know they objected to it in relation to his evidence, but she strays from that into conclusions based upon evidence supplied to her.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: They objected as to foundation and we then required, of course, Dr. Gow, before he gave an opinion, to express or to delineate the basis of his opinion. Of course, now we also have in evidence the last day of Dr. Gow's testimony. The Prosecutor offered sections of the Commission of Experts Report, two different reports, as to the presence of paramilitary. That came in and that, of course, is based upon -- as a matter of fact, the footnotes were missing; I would like to see the footnotes because that is the basis for the report, but most of the Dr. Gow's testimony, the last day, was based upon, at least, sources of all kind, including the two reports from the Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One from the Secretary General, I was here on that occasion, and those matters were produced in cross-examination, because what was being challenged was some of his conclusions that he was presenting to the court based upon his research. So he was being cross-examined upon the Secretary General's report.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, I was not referring to the Secretary General's report; I was referring to the two reports from the Commission of Experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But we are going beyond this, beyond looking at newspapers and reviewing and surveying what was happening in the Belgrade press, what was happening in the other press, what was coming out of radio stations, TV stations, where an historian is perfectly properly able to give a commentary as to what he was hearing. We are getting here right into the evidence, from evidence relating to an attack at Hambarine at a checkpoint with comment about it, to evidence relating to a small band of poorly armed Muslims and Croats entered Prijedor town in an attempt to recapture Prijedor. This is comment. This is not Dr. Gow's research. This is comment upon evidence that the court will hear and will have to make its own findings upon. That is why I say, well, where do we limit this? Do we apply the same standards and call investigators (because that is really what this witness is, she is an investigator) to counter this in relation to objectives in the case that we see important. I hope that assists the court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have anything else, Mr. Tieger? Two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour, and I will be quick. It is very convenient for the Defence to characterise her as an investigator; that is not what she is. I point to the Defence comment, should we produce a couple of investigators to say that the accused is not guilty? That exactly highlights the fallacy of their argument in two respects; if they can produce someone who is tasked by the world community to become an expert on this subject and who reviewed every bit of available data to do so, which is basically what an historical expert does, then they have a different argument. Furthermore, she is not offering an opinion one way or another about this accused's specific involvement, or offering an opinion about his guilt or innocence. Again the Defence tries to suggest that the court needs no assistance with what happened in this opstina because you will hear all about it from witnesses. The fact of the matter, as I tried to emphasise, this is an extensive systematic and widespread activity over a large area. Each witness can only see a slice of that. We did not select witnesses for that particular purpose, but witnesses who had evidence about the accused's involvement directly and about the accused specifically, that is not what this witness will testify to. The irony that appears here is that the Defence says, we have no objection about hearing everything she learned from other sources, and she certainly a sufficient expert to testify before the court relying on those matters, but we do not want to hear if she learned anything from independent investigations which included information obtained from people all over the world which, I submit, is exactly the kind of information that historians typically rely on. If it turns out that a particular opinion of hers is based exclusively on that kind of data, this court is certainly in a position to give it whatever amount of weight it feels is appropriate. This court should not turn its back on the opportunity to hear from the very person who was asked by the community of nations to find out what happened there.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess until 2.30. When we return, Mr. Wladimiroff will be here, will he not, Mr. Orie?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That is what I expect, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will meet in camera for a few minutes to discuss the trial schedule. Then we will resume in open court to discuss the offer of proof as well as the objection. We stand in recess then until 2.00. (1.15 p.m.) (Luncheon Adjournment) (IN CLOSED SESSION) (2.30 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (IN OPEN SESSION)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Now we are in open session. Before the lunch recess, we heard an objection to the testimony of Miss Hanne Sophie Greve -- is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Greve", your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Greve. The Prosecutor made a proffer of the testimony that would be offered and the Defence objected and submitted a two or three-page brief for us to read as well as attachments from rules of evidence of national systems. As I said, as we said in our opening remarks, this is not a national system. We are guided by our Rules of Procedure and Evidence that the Tribunal has developed. When we have in Rule 89(A), when it provides that the Chamber shall not be bound by national rules of evidence, that is intentional, that was deliberate, on the part of drafters of the rules. So we consider that we look to our rules of evidence to determine whether or not evidence is admissible. Rules 89 of our rules of evidence, of course, is the guiding rule. 89(C) provides that a Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. We consider that, based on the proffer of the Prosecutor and considering the objections of the Defence, the testimony of Miss Greve certainly is relevant and it appears that it has probative value. Under Rule 89(D), the Chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. So that our determination at this time that the testimony is relevant, and that it appears to have probative value, does not in any way bind the Trial Chamber from excluding the testimony, should we make such a determination after hearing the testimony and hearing the context in which it is given. We are very cognizant of the fact that we are judges, experienced judges. We are not a jury. We believe we can listen to this testimony that we consider to be relevant and appears to have probative value, and give it the appropriate weight that is necessary. So would you call your witness, please, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. The Prosecution calls Hanne Sophie Greve. JUDGE HANNE SOPHIE GREVE, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: There should be an oath there, Miss Greve, if you would take the oath, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, you may be seated, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Examined by MR. TIEGER

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hanne Sophie Greve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are currently sitting as a judge in the Court of Appeals for Western Norway; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have been since 1988?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also serve and have served as a trial judge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you taught law as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you served in the Faculty of Law at the University of Bergen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to your basic degree in law, have you attained an advanced degree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask what your doctoral thesis was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It has a double title; it is called “Kampucean Refugees: Between the Tiger and the Crocodile", that is an Eastern proverb, International Law and the overall scope of one refugee's situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you do not mind, I will address you by your academic title during the course of these proceedings rather than your judicial title?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to your career in law in Norway, have you been extensively involved in efforts surrounding international humanitarian rights violations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to tell the court briefly about those activities and, perhaps, I can lead you through them so we can move forward quickly. Were you an assistant protection officer for the UNHCR in Thailand for two years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was in 1979 and in 1981?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your work focused primarily on Cambodian refugees; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After completing that duty, did you receive a grant to conduct research into the circumstances of such refugees and continue your work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you conduct a fact finding mission to Ethiopia for Save the Children in 1985?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that concern problems relating to children left on their own in the emergency of famine and war in Ethiopia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you conduct a fact finding mission to Angola for the Lutheran World Federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In so doing, were you looking into allegations of serious human rights violations by SWAPO against its own people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you conduct a fact finding mission to Cambodia and Thailand on behalf of the Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that for the possibility of determining whether humanitarian aid -- the possibility of repatriation existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you organise the election monitoring system for Romania?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was one of the key persons in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then serve as on scene election observer in Romania in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that done with the co-operation of the Helsinki Federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it done upon a formal invitation from Romania?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that same system, that is, the one which you helped to organise and implement in Romania later adopted for Lithuania and Latvia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you serve as on scene election observer in those countries as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you write the first prison profile covering prisons, which included political refugees in connection with Thailand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In connection with Cambodia and the People's Republic of Cambodia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that sent to the High Commissioner of Refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as well as Amnesty International.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you taught land law in Cambodia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you served as a human rights researcher for the Christie Mickelson Institute in Norway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, in 1992, did the Security Council of the United Nations express its grave alarm at continuing reports of widespread violations of international humanitarian law occurring in the territory of former Yugoslavia and especially in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result, was a resolution adopted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that call upon international humanitarian organisations to collate substantiated information in their possession and make it available to a Commission of Experts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the same resolution did the United Nations establish an impartial Commission of Experts to examine and analyse that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As well as any further information which the Commission might obtain through its own efforts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that done pursuant to Chapter 7 of the Charter of the United Nations which provides for the Security Council to take special measures when there is a threat to peace, a breach of the peace or international aggression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have a document presented to the witness?
